title: A typed path parameter
options: The handler receives the string.
The framework returns a validation error (422).
The route returns 404.
explanation: FastAPI validates a declared integer path parameter before calling the handler. A non-integer value causes a 422 response.
hint: The annotation is part of the request contract.

title: A missing optional query
options: {"limit": 0}
{"limit": 10}
The request must include limit.
explanation: A query parameter with a default is optional. Omitting it uses the declared default, 10.
hint: Look for the default value after the equals sign.

title: Bound a page size
options: 500 is silently clamped to 50.
The handler receives 500.
The request fails validation (422).
explanation: Query bounds reject values outside the accepted range; they do not clamp the caller’s input.
hint: What do ge and le describe?

title: A deliberate missing record
options: Raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Missing") to return a 404.
Returning an error dictionary automatically sets 404.
Use a print statement to set the status.
explanation: Returning an ordinary dictionary normally produces a 200 response. Raise HTTPException to set the intended error status.
hint: A response body does not determine its HTTP status.

title: Validate a request body
options: A product is created with a negative price.
Body validation fails before creation.
status_code=201 disables validation.
explanation: The Pydantic model validates the JSON request body. Field(gt=0) requires a positive price.
hint: Check the constraint on price.

title: Avoid blocking an async route
options: Use await asyncio.sleep(2) for a non-blocking delay.
async def makes time.sleep non-blocking.
Run an endless loop to keep the server busy.
explanation: time.sleep blocks the event-loop thread. An awaited asynchronous operation lets the loop handle other work during the wait.
hint: async def does not transform synchronous calls automatically.

title: Finish a JSON response
options: Call res.end() when the response is complete.
Call console.log() to close the socket.
JSON.stringify closes the response.
explanation: write sends bytes without ending the response. end marks the response as complete so the client can finish reading it.
hint: Which API signals that no more body data is coming?

title: A query is not the pathname
code:
// req.url is /api/products?inStock=true
if (req.url === "/api/products") { /* ... */ }
options: Use new URL(req.url, "http://localhost").pathname for route matching.
Use req.url.toUpperCase().
Remove all routing and return the same response.
explanation: The raw URL includes its query string. Parse it, then use pathname for the route and searchParams for filters.
hint: Separate the path from its query parameters.

title: Promise or timer first?
options: start, timer, promise, end
start, end, promise, timer
start, end, timer, promise
explanation: Synchronous statements finish first. The resolved promise callback runs as a microtask before the timer callback in this example.
hint: A zero-millisecond timer is still asynchronous.

title: Await the request
options: Add await before fetch.
Remove async from load.
Use JSON.stringify(response).
explanation: fetch returns a Promise. Await it to obtain a Response before calling json(). Also handle non-success HTTP statuses in real code.
hint: Which value has the json method?

title: Bound a request body
options: Count incoming bytes and reject a body over the limit.
Only inspect Content-Length, even if it is absent.
Convert every chunk to uppercase.
explanation: Enforce a byte limit while reading the stream, including when Content-Length is missing or inaccurate. Reject an oversized body before parsing it.
hint: Limits must apply to the bytes actually received.

title: Return a meaningful status
code:
res.writeHead(200, {"Content-Type":"application/json"});
res.end(JSON.stringify({error:"Product not found"}));
options: Use a 404 response status for a missing product.
JSON error keys automatically change the status.
Use 201 for a missing product.
explanation: An error-shaped JSON body can still be an HTTP success. Set the correct status so clients can use response.ok and error handling.
hint: Status and body are separate parts of HTTP.

title: Find missing values
code: SELECT * FROM products WHERE category = NULL;
options: Use category IS NULL.
Use category == NULL.
NULL equals every value.
explanation: NULL represents an unknown or missing value. Equality with NULL is not true; use IS NULL to test for it.
hint: SQL uses three-valued logic.

title: Keep data out of SQL text
code: const sql = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE title = '" + title + "'";
options: Use a parameterised query with a $1 placeholder and a separate values array.
Escape only spaces.
Trust every value from a form.
explanation: Parameterised queries keep user values separate from SQL syntax. String concatenation can turn a value into executable SQL.
hint: Data should be supplied separately from the query string.

title: Read a JSONB property
code:
SELECT metadata->>'color' AS color
FROM products WHERE id = 1;
options: A text value such as green.
The whole database.
Always a JSON array.
explanation: The ->> operator extracts a JSON property as text. The -> operator retains a JSON value.
hint: Notice the second greater-than sign.

title: Query PostgreSQL products
code: SELECT * FROM products;
solution: SELECT id, title FROM products WHERE stock > 0 ORDER BY id;
goal: Return id and title for products in stock, ordered by id.
explanation: Return id and title for products in stock, ordered by id. This activity executes in a disposable PGlite PostgreSQL engine on your device.
hint: Use the table explorer and select only the requested columns.

title: Investigate JSONB data
code: SELECT * FROM products;
solution: SELECT title, metadata->>'color' AS color FROM products WHERE metadata->>'color' = 'green';
goal: Return title and color as text for the green product.
explanation: Return title and color as text for the green product. This activity executes in a disposable PGlite PostgreSQL engine on your device.
hint: Use the table explorer and select only the requested columns.

title: Rank the product prices
code: SELECT * FROM products;
solution: SELECT title, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY price DESC)::int AS price_rank FROM products ORDER BY price DESC;
goal: Return title and an integer price_rank, most expensive first. Use row_number over price descending.
explanation: Return title and an integer price_rank, most expensive first. Use row_number over price descending. This activity executes in a disposable PGlite PostgreSQL engine on your device.
hint: Use the table explorer and select only the requested columns.

title: Start small, then expand
code: ...
options: One column by default; two from the md breakpoint upwards.
Two columns only on phones.
Two columns at every width.
explanation: Unprefixed classes apply by default. The md variant applies at the medium breakpoint and larger widths.
hint: Tailwind responsive variants are mobile-first.

title: A visible keyboard focus
code: <button class="outline-none">Save</button>
options: Add an intentional focus-visible outline or ring.
Remove the button’s label.
Hide the button when it receives focus.
explanation: Removing an outline without a replacement makes keyboard focus difficult to find. Supply a visible focus style with sufficient contrast.
hint: Keyboard users need to know which control is active.

title: A class the build cannot see
code: const className = `bg-${color}-500`;
options: Map allowed colors to complete class strings such as bg-green-500.
Every possible interpolated class is always generated.
Add arbitrary user input as a class name.
explanation: Production builds detect complete class names in source. Map options to full classes so the needed utilities are present.
hint: Can the scanner see bg-green-500 as a complete string?

title: Centre a Tailwind card
code: <main data-target class="min-h-[240px] bg-lime-50"><article class="rounded-2xl bg-white p-6">A little idea</article></main>
solution: <main data-target class="flex min-h-[240px] items-center justify-center bg-lime-50"><article class="rounded-2xl bg-white p-6">A little idea</article></main>
goal: Give the stage flex layout, centre its children on both axes, and use a 240px minimum height.
explanation: Give the stage flex layout, centre its children on both axes, and use a 240px minimum height. Checks inspect computed styles generated by the actual Tailwind browser engine.
hint: Edit complete utility class names on the element marked data-target.

title: Two columns with utilities
code: <main data-target class="bg-lime-50 p-4"><article class="rounded-xl bg-white p-6">One</article><article class="rounded-xl bg-white p-6">Two</article></main>
solution: <main data-target class="grid grid-cols-2 gap-4 bg-lime-50 p-4"><article class="rounded-xl bg-white p-6">One</article><article class="rounded-xl bg-white p-6">Two</article></main>
goal: Set the stage to a two-column grid with a 16px gap.
explanation: Set the stage to a two-column grid with a 16px gap. Checks inspect computed styles generated by the actual Tailwind browser engine.
hint: Edit complete utility class names on the element marked data-target.

title: Style an accessible action
code: <button data-target class="bg-green-800 px-6 text-white">Keep learning</button>
solution: <button data-target class="min-h-12 rounded-xl bg-green-800 px-6 font-bold text-white focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-4">Keep learning</button>
goal: Give the button a bold font, a 12px radius and a 48px minimum height. Keep its label.
explanation: Give the button a bold font, a 12px radius and a 48px minimum height. Keep its label. Checks inspect computed styles generated by the actual Tailwind browser engine.
hint: Edit complete utility class names on the element marked data-target.

title: Transform an array
code:
<?php
$values = [1, 2, 3];
$result = array_map(fn($n) => $n * 2, $values);
echo json_encode($result);
options: null
explanation: array_map returns a new array of callback results. Each number is multiplied by two, and json_encode serialises that array.
hint: Apply the callback to each element.

title: A safe optional field
code:
<?php
$user = ["name" => "Asha"];
echo $user["city"] ?? "Unknown";
options: Unknown
An empty array
A fatal exception
explanation: The null-coalescing operator supplies the fallback when the array key is missing or null.
hint: Which expression is on the right of ??

title: Avoid a loose comparison
code:
<?php
$enabled = "0";
if ($enabled == false) { echo "off"; }
options: Use an explicit input contract and strict comparisons when types matter.
== never converts types.
All non-empty strings are true in PHP, including "0".
explanation: Loose comparison performs coercion. PHP also treats the string "0" as falsy. Validate the input format, then compare the intended types explicitly.
hint: The special string "0" is an important PHP edge case.

title: Reject malformed JSON
code:
<?php
$input = json_decode($raw, true);
// How should malformed JSON be handled?
options: Use JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR and catch JsonException.
Treat every null result as a valid object.
Print the request into an HTML page without escaping.
explanation: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR distinguishes malformed JSON from a legitimate JSON null. Validate that a decoded request has the expected object shape.
hint: Parsing and validating the resulting shape are different steps.

title: Preserve a JSON list
code:
<?php
$rows = [0 => "A", 1 => "B", 2 => "C"];
$filtered = array_filter($rows, fn($v) => $v !== "B");
echo json_encode($filtered);
options: Use array_values($filtered) before JSON encoding if a JSON array is required.
array_filter always reindexes numeric keys.
json_encode removes every key automatically.
explanation: array_filter preserves keys. Non-contiguous numeric keys encode as a JSON object; array_values reindexes them into a list.
hint: The retained keys are 0 and 2.

title: Display user text safely
code: <?php echo $name; ?>
options: Escape HTML output with htmlspecialchars($name, ENT_QUOTES | ENT_SUBSTITUTE, "UTF-8").
Trust all names because they are short.
Use JSON encoding as a universal HTML escaping solution.
explanation: Use context-appropriate escaping when outputting user text into HTML. htmlspecialchars handles the HTML text context; other contexts need their own handling.
hint: The destination is HTML, not a JSON response.

title: A route parameter
options: The placeholder supplies the value 7 to the handler.
The handler always receives the entire URL.
The parameter is an automatic SQL query.
explanation: A route placeholder supplies its matched segment to the handler. A typed Eloquent model would enable model binding, but this example uses a string.
hint: Look at the placeholder and handler parameter.

title: Validate a price
options: Validation rejects the negative price.
The title rule converts the price to zero.
Validation is skipped for JSON.
explanation: The gt:0 rule requires a positive value. JSON clients should send Accept: application/json to receive JSON validation responses.
hint: Read the numeric constraint after required.

title: Created means 201
code: return response()->json($product); // a newly created resource
options: Pass 201 as the second argument for the intended created status.
The word product changes the status automatically.
Always return 500 after creation.
explanation: A JSON body and its status are separate. response()->json($product, 201) explicitly marks successful creation.
hint: The default success status is not Created.

title: Accept only intended fields
code: Product::create($request->all());
options: Validate allowed fields and configure model assignment rules.
Trust all submitted properties.
Rename the request variable to make it safe.
explanation: A client can submit unexpected properties. Use validated fields and deliberate fillable/guarded configuration instead of treating the whole request as trusted data.
hint: Should a client be able to set owner_id or is_admin?

title: A missing model
code:
$product = Product::findOrFail($id);
 // No product has this id.
options: Laravel can turn the model-not-found exception into a 404 response.
It silently inserts a new product.
It returns the first product instead.
explanation: findOrFail throws when the record is absent. The framework exception handler translates an uncaught model-not-found exception to a not-found response.
hint: The OrFail suffix describes the missing-record path.

title: Load relationships deliberately
options: Consider eager loading with Order::with("customer")->get().
Run one extra query per order on purpose.
Add a CSS class to reduce SQL queries.
explanation: Accessing an unloaded relationship in a loop can cause one query per order. Eager loading fetches the relationship for the collection deliberately.
hint: Think about when customer is loaded.
